wp.claude: The first thing I noticed was the baby powder. We don't have a baby. Now she came down to the kitchen at seven like something exhumed, eyes swollen, hair flattened on one side and wild on the other, and she drank her coffee standing at the counter with both hands around the mug as if it might try to escape. Their lights glowed and their compressors hummed, and the Funyuns and Snickers and Diet Pepsis sat in their coils, visible behind the glass. Nobody could get them. Pry bars bent. By noon all forty-one machines on my route had gone still and bright, and the radio was saying it wasn't just here, it was everywhere. wp.claude: The registry clerk didn't look up when she stamped my file. She held my hand through cotton for a year before she got used to it. You get used to anything.

wp.glm: The trick to a professional fall is choosing your animal. Anybody can climb a rail. The art is in the landing. Six years in the trade. Ostriches are solid value — they look deranged on camera, and the worst you take home is a bruise shaped like Tasmania. Camels are excellent: forty-five seconds of looming and spitting, maximum drama, zero stitches. Tapirs if you're desperate. Big cats are for people with death wishes and better lawyers than mine, and nobody takes gorilla gigs anymore — one bad afternoon in 2016 closed that whole line of work. We don't talk about it. There's a candle about it. The economics are simple. You fall, you get rescued, the zoo shuts down for two days, the safety review makes the evening news, the lawsuits bloom like algae, and attendance drops six percent for a season. I’d been a dockworker for twenty years, a lifetime measured in the heft of crates and the groan of timber. It wasn't glamorous, but it was honest. Or it *had* been. Lately, everything felt…off. wp.claude: Spurinna had been reading livers for forty years, and in all that time he had never once seen the future in one. He saw other things. He knew the bronze map of the liver as well as he knew the roads of his own Tarquinia: the sixteen houses of the gods along the rim, the gall bladder where Tinia lived, the lobe that belonged to the dead. He could point to any fold of purple meat and tell a nervous magistrate which god was frowning at him and why. He was very good at it. The Romans paid an Etruscan to do it because they believed the Etruscans had been born knowing how, the way fish are born knowing water. What Spurinna actually knew was people. A haruspex is a kind of confessor.

Cassius, who watches a room like a man pricing it. Cimber, with his aggrieved little cough. Trebonius, punctual to a fault — he had been punctual in my classroom, years ago, when I taught him the Greek future tense and he asked me why anyone would bother learning a tense for things that had not yet happened. I should have recognized the omen in the question. Six of the eight had sat in my school. I am a teacher of rhetoric. I want that understood plainly, because everything that follows depends on it: I had spent thirty years in Rome instructing the sons of great men in the arrangement of arguments, the seduction of an audience, the placing of one word before another so that the hearer cannot help but follow.

Most people, I’d learned, found comfort in sudden bursts of melody. A joyful jig during a good meal, a mournful ballad when a loved one departed, a triumphant chorus after a hard-won victory. They *sang*. I, however, could not. It wasn’t a medical condition, not exactly. Doctors had poked, prodded, scanned, and theorized. Neurologists, psychologists, even a particularly eccentric ethnomusicologist. They’d concluded it was… anomalous. A genetic quirk. A complete and utter failure of the “spontaneous song gene.” I was a human anomaly, a beige blot in a world saturated with color – specifically, the color of song. It hadn’t always been this isolating. As a child, it was terrifying. Birthdays were excruciating. Christmas carols felt like an assault. Even simple things, like a particularly beautiful sunset, threatened to erupt into a full-blown operatic aria in my head. My parents, bless their anxious hearts, tried everything.
wp.claude: The first time I understood, I was six, and my grandfather's dog had been hit by a truck on Route 9. My cousin Bethany, who was five, stood in the gravel at the end of the driveway and opened her mouth, and what came out was a ballad. A real one, with verses. The wind came up behind her on the second line like it had been waiting in the wings. Somewhere a cello I could not locate began to play. My aunt came off the porch harmonizing, and my grandfather, who I had never once seen cry, took the bridge in a baritone that made the corn lean toward him. I stood there with my mouth open too. Nothing came out. I tried. I pushed at the place in my chest where the bad feeling was, the way you push at a stuck drawer, and it stayed stuck. When it was over, the cello stopped, and everyone wiped their faces and felt better. You could see it on them, the way you can see that someone has eaten.
wp.glm: The morning my neighborhood sang about the new traffic circle, I stood at the edge of it with my groceries, waiting for a break in the choreography. The roundabout went in on a Tuesday and by Wednesday it had a melody — something in a bright 6/8, mail carriers waltzing their routes, the crossing guard conducting with her stop sign, two sparrows on the signal box taking the descant and somebody's terrier on the oohs. Three verses. A bridge about roundabouts being nature's way of saying we'll get there when we get there. I crossed during the instrumental. A woman in a bathrobe caught my hands on the second chorus — "You know the words!" — and pulled me in, and the music crashed into my quiet and died, and she stood there holding my hands in the sudden embarrassing silence, and then let go. That's the other thing about me, the thing that gets me disinvited from weddings. Where I walk, the music thins. Within about four steps the orchestra loses its nerve; within arm's reach it stops altogether.

wp.human: It was Summer. I had returned from the grocery store where I purchased all of my provisions for the month, when I hear a knock at my door. I assumed it was her. I remember smiling to myself as I walked toward the door. My smile was removed as suddenly as the door was from its frame. Six agents of the GSB (Governement Servitude Bureau) rushed in, tackled me to the ground while screaming; "You are under arrest as you have been chosen as a representative of government! Keep still or we'll blow your fucking brains on the wall!" Terrified, shaking with the fear and shock of the event, I slowly felt the recognition of my fate. I have been called into government servitude. The alarm went off as it always did at 5 A.M. Slowly, with no sudden movements, I put on my politicians jumpsuit under the ever-watching eye of the camera and the Stunner. I put the nightmare behind me, as I always did, and prepared for my day.
wp.gemma: The rain was always a pale, filtered grey. It didn’t fall with a crash or a rumble, but rather a slow, insistent weeping that coated everything in a shimmering, uniform dampness. It was, according to the Informational Displays, perfectly calibrated to maintain atmospheric equilibrium and prevent the proliferation of mold. I’d never seen a truly dark cloud, never felt the sting of a heavy downpour. Just this perpetual, gentle sorrow. My designation was Unit 734, but everyone called me Seven. Names were inefficient. Efficiency was everything. I worked in Sector Gamma, Level 4, Processing – specifically, the meticulous arrangement of nutrient paste. It came in five shades of beige: Pale, Mid-Tone, Standard, Rich, and Umber. Each shade was precisely measured, dispensed, and assigned to a citizen based on their biometric data and predicted caloric needs. Deviation was… discouraged. Life in the Collective was, objectively, comfortable. The Housing Modules were compact but spotless, equipped with sonic dampeners and automated sanitation systems. Food, while monotonous, was nutritious and devoid of any unpleasant textures or flavors.
wp.claude: The Wardens came for Ilan three times that winter. The first time, he hadn't left his flat in four days. He heard the knock, the patient double rap they all used, and he sat very still on the floor beneath the window with the radio pressed against his chest, its dial turned down to nothing. The knocking stopped. Something was set down on the step. When he finally looked, it was a covered dish of barley stew, still warm, and a note in a round hand: *Your Ledger's been empty. We'll come again Thursday.* He did not eat the stew. He knew how these things worked. The Outside broadcasts had explained it, late at night, in their smooth and sorrowful voices: the regime watches. The regime logs every hour of your life on a public board in the square. When you stop producing, they come. The second time, he answered the door, because he was afraid of what would happen if he didn't.
wp.glm: The dossier listed twelve indicators of tyranny. Walls: yes. Curfews: yes. Controlled borders, rationing, marked citizens, state ownership of the dead, disappearances beginning in old age. Eleven were confirmed before I ever saw the place. I was sent to document the twelfth. From the road, Greyhollow did not disappoint. Concrete the color of old weather. Watchtowers. Floodlights mounted along the wall, pointing outward, which the dossier's authors had surely meant as aggression. A crowd pressed against the gate, hundreds deep, faces upturned. I approached the fence expecting weeping, expecting hands thrust through the wire. A boy tugged my sleeve. "Is it Wednesday?" he asked. "They post the list on Wednesdays." A woman with a steward's armband was pinning paper to a board: names, dozens of them. The crowd murmured. A man whooped at his own; a family embraced strangers. Down the line, others ladled soup into tin cups, and a girl offered me a stub of chalk. "To hold places," she said. "Pell's is the tall mark. Don't smudge it."

wp.human: The steel gates of the dark fortress crashed to the floor, and a figure clad in an immaculate white cloak and shining silver armor stepped into the great hall. This was the champion of light, and he had come to the fortress to stop the dark lord of the land once and for all. The figure’s sword glowed with a radiant light that pierced the darkness of the hall illuminating a swarming mass of the dark lord’s servants. Goblins, trolls, and undead thralls rushed towards the unwelcomed visitor while witches and fiends casted unholy magics towards the entranceway. The spells bounced harmlessly off the hero’s armor, and with one swift motion of his wrist, lightning, brighter than the sun, flew from the sword and coursed through the approaching horde. The lightning turned all of the hall’s visible occupants into dust, but stopped at the other end of the hall where an unwavering shadow dissipated the lightning’s energy. The champion strolled towards the shadow.
wp.gemma: The air in the Obsidian Chamber tasted of ozone and simmering rage. It was a surprisingly pleasant combination, considering the circumstances. Crimson light pulsed from the heart of the room – a massive, geometrically unsettling construct of polished black obsidian, humming with barely contained power. And, predictably, standing before it, radiating a barely-controlled fury, was Silas Vane. I, Captain Rex “Renegade” Harding, veteran of a thousand skirmishes and possessor of a remarkably durable jawline, burst through the reinforced steel doors with the practiced ease of a man accustomed to ignoring warning signs. My pulse hammered against my ribs, a familiar rhythm of adrenaline and grim determination. Vane was a menace. A brilliant, calculating, utterly ruthless menace who’d been systematically dismantling the energy grids of the Eastern Seaboard for the past six months, all to fund his… eccentric collection of rare and aggressively grumpy gemstones. “Vane!” I roared, drawing my plasma rifle. “It ends here! Your reign of disruption stops now!” Vane didn’t flinch. He simply turned, a slight, almost bored expression on his face.
wp.claude: The skylight came down in a sheet of glittering fragments, and Lodestar came down with it. She'd practiced the landing. One knee, one fist, cape settling a half-second after the rest of her, like punctuation. The floor of the lair cracked in a satisfying starburst. Somewhere behind her, the last of the glass tinkled against the stone. "Count Ashgrave," she said, rising. "Your reign of terror ends tonight." The lair was everything she'd been told to expect. Vaulted ceilings, green-tinged lighting, a vast machine humming at the far end of the chamber with a countdown clock blinking above it in red: 00:41:17. Banks of monitors. A throne made from what looked like melted-down church bells. Count Ashgrave was not on the throne. He was sitting on the bottom step of the dais in a grey cardigan, phone pressed to his ear, holding up one finger. "One moment," he said. Lodestar stared at him. "Yes, I'm still here," Ashgrave said into the phone. "No, I don't want to be transferred again.
wp.glm: Comet hit the skylight at midnight, because doom did not keep business hours. She came down through a thunder of her own making, landed in the three-point stance that eleven years of hero work had perfected, and rose with light crackling off her fists. Doctor Havoc's lair spread out before her: obsidian floors, cables thick as anacondas feeding the great humming heart of the Tempest Engine, and the man himself on the dais in his storm-grey armor, one finger raised in the middle of a lecture. Comet braced for the monologue. She had a counter-monologue prepared. What she did not have was preparation for the finger to be pointed—not at her, but at a sixteen-year-old girl sitting on a crate of plasma lances, drinking a blue slushie. Nobody had noticed Comet at all. "You said front row," the girl said. "You said, quote, 'nothing short of the apocalypse could keep me away.'" "There *was* an apocalypse in Sector Seven—" "A satellite, Dad. You stole a *satellite*. Regionals happens once a year." "The ionosphere belongs to no one, Delia."

wp.human: "Y'know Larry, people seem really concerned about us selling private information to third parties," I say with a worried look on my face. "We say'Don't Be Evil,' but aren't we really being evil if we're doing something that people don't want us to?" Larry looks up excitedly "That's it! We stop selling information to third parties!" That was a lot easier than I expected. It was Larry's idea that we should sell custom advertising rights in the first place to avoid having our users pay. I mean, we make a ton of money anyway, why would we need any more? Larry continues after contemplating, "We'll just sell people automated services for money; we've got the best computer scientists in the world so there's no way we can't automate everything." Yea, Larry was being Larry. He always seemed to have his mind on his money, but what could you do about it? At least we would stop selling private information and we'd even be working on some cool new projects. "That sounds great!" I reply.
wp.gemma: The rain tasted like lubricant. Not a particularly unpleasant lubricant, mind you – a clean, slightly citrusy blend designed to neutralize atmospheric pollutants and, apparently, enhance the palate. It was the standard issue rain in Sector 7, delivered via the Atmospheric Regulation Drones, affectionately known as “Rainbirds.” Everything in Neo-Veridia, and indeed, the entire planet, was delivered by Rainbirds. Everything. My name is Silas Vance, and I’m a Data Retriever. It’s a remarkably dull job, truthfully. I sift through the endless stream of sensory data collected by the OmniCorp network – everything from the temperature of a loaf of Synth-Bread to the emotional state of a sanitation worker – searching for anomalies. Anything that deviates from the perfectly calibrated, relentlessly optimized norms dictated by OmniCorp. Today, it was a report of a single, wilting dandelion pushing through a crack in the pavement. Dandelions. They hadn’t been seen in Neo-Veridia for seventy-three years. Not officially, anyway. OmniCorp’s control was absolute. Seventy-three years ago, the “Great Reorganization” had begun, spearheaded by the charismatic, impossibly young CEO, Elias Thorne.
wp.claude: The Acquisitions Department of Consolidated occupied half of the fourth floor of a building in Duluth, and in the eleven years Margit Oduya had worked there it had acquired nothing. This was not a failing. Her performance reviews said so every spring, in the same warm, automated language: *Margit continues to meet all targets for her role.* The targets were zero. Everything on Earth had belonged to Consolidated since the Final Merger, forty-one years earlier, when the last independent concern on the planet, a cooperative bakery in Tromsø, had signed its papers and been handed a small ceremonial check that it deposited, of course, in a Consolidated bank. After that there was nothing left to buy. But the bylaws required an Acquisitions Department, and nobody at Consolidated changed the bylaws, because the bylaws were the only thing Consolidated didn't own. They were what owned Consolidated. So the department remained: four desks, a fern, a fax machine kept for reasons of tradition, and Mr.
wp.glm: The Company had never stolen anything. That was the problem. In four hundred years it had only ever bought. It bought the continents first, quietly, then the oceans above the seabed it already owned. It bought the weather, which it dispensed by subscription, and the night, which it rented back at a premium to anyone who wanted to see stars. It bought the more useful letters of the alphabet. It bought the surnames of nearly everyone alive — mine included; I lease mine back for weddings and funerals — and when a family fell behind, they became numbers, and the numbers were owned too. By the time I was promoted to Final Acquisitions, the audit read 99.9999999 percent. One line short. The ninth CEO had already approved the press release, drafted a decade earlier and updated quarterly, waiting on a single number to become true: ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING ON EARTH BELONGS TO THE COMPANY. The open line in the Ledger read: Asset: a promise. Status: kept. Holder: none. Kept by: Mercer, Nell, 89. Location: well no. 112, Halvorsen County.

wp.human: The sleek whiteness of the walls hurt. All the government buildings were designed to hurt. The adjudicators were ushered into the sleek, white changing rooms where they changed into tight black jumpsuits. The jumpsuits hurt. The women's hair was pinned up so as not to betray sensibilities and everyone's faces were examined for any telling signs of preference. "Juror # 44A," resounded a voice from everywhere. The sound hurt. "Please step forward for evaluation." I stepped into the evaluation chamber. It was the only part of the building that didn't hurt. It had a cool black interior, cylindrical with a single protuberance. "Juror, please, bite down on the groove." I did as the voice commanded. A red light slowly crawled up the black walls. "Reminder to all Jurors: personal biases are okay." Once the red light finished its slow trek, a buzzer sounded and the door opened.
wp.gemma: The rain smelled of rust and regret, a fitting accompaniment to the grey dread that clung to my skin. Ten years. Ten years since the last evaluation, ten years since I’d last felt the tremor of hope – a foolish, dangerous sentiment – before the panel. Ten years since I’d last truly *lived*. I adjusted the worn wool of my tunic, pulling it tighter against the damp chill of the Citadel’s courtyard. Around me, the others shuffled, a restless sea of faces etched with similar anxieties. We were all ‘Presented,’ designated by the Council to endure this…ritual. Presented to be judged, to be deemed worthy of continued existence. The Council’s pronouncements were absolute. Every decade, they assessed the collective ‘Worth’ of the population. Based on a complex, inscrutable algorithm – whispered to be a blend of productivity, social contribution, and perceived ‘resonance’ – individuals were marked as ‘Impressive’ or ‘Insufficient.’ The Insufficient were…disposed of. Not with grand, theatrical executions, but with a cold, clinical efficiency. A single dose of Null, administered by a silent attendant, and they were gone.
wp.claude: The waiting room had no clocks, which Dell thought was cruel until she realized it was a kindness. Nobody wanted to watch the minutes go by in here. There were six other people on the benches, all of them turning forty this week, all of them dressed like they were going to a funeral or a job interview. The man across from her was moving his lips silently, rehearsing. A woman near the door had brought a binder. Dell had brought nothing. She had a napkin from the hospital cafeteria folded in her coat pocket, and she kept touching it like a coin. "Okafor, Adele." The review chamber was small and white, with a single chair facing a long table. Behind the table sat three people. Each was her. Everyone knew how it worked, but knowing didn't help. At every review, the state recorded you: your memories, your opinions, your voice, all the ugly furniture of your mind at that exact age. Then that recording took a seat on every board you would ever face.
wp.glm: The letters come in stiff cream envelopes, your name in type so formal it could be a summons from God. One at twenty. Another at thirty. My mother received five. My grandmother, seven. My sister June received three. Evaluation Day works like this: you stand in a gray room before a board of seven, strangers born in your year, drawn by lottery. People who stood in your queues, who remember your graduations, who know exactly how ordinary you are. They read your decade aloud like a grocery list, and then they vote. If you have impressed your peers, you go home. If you haven't, you are executed at dusk. Humanely. That word is in the pamphlet too. *Impress your peers* — as though life were a talent show where the prize is another audition. No one remembers who built it. It judged our grandmothers' grandmothers. There is no arguing with a thing that old; you can only stand where it tells you.

wp.human: As you travel through the woods just outside the large village of Rushire, you hear a man call out to you from off the trail. "You! Yes! You there, I need your help! Please, I know I look like shit right now but, try, just try and look past that, okay? I've just been through Hell. No, that's not right. Hell has been *through me. *" You take a good look at the man who has come running up to you. He stinks so bad you want to wretch. He appears to be wearing nothing but animal furs for clothes and a pair of worn sandles woven from dried grass on his feet. His hair, both on his head and his face, is wild, long, and dirty. Caked with bits of dried mud and something darker. His body is thin and looks starved. His eyes are wide open and never seem to stop glancing around. The man looks panic stricken, but has an air of intensity about him.
wp.gemma: The rain was a greasy smear on the window, mirroring the feeling in my gut. It wasn’t just the storm, though the wind howled like a wounded beast, rattling the loose panes of the apartment building. It was *him*. Or, rather, the insistent, oily pressure at the back of my skull. He called himself Silas. A voice, initially, a low hum beneath the constant chatter of the others. But he was getting louder, sharper, a deliberate insistence that clawed at the edges of my thoughts. He wanted in. He wanted *me*. Schizophrenia had been a slow, insidious thief, stripping away the colors of my world until everything was viewed through a fractured, distorted lens. The voices weren’t new; they'd been a constant companion for years – the Gardener, meticulously pruning the roses in my mental garden with a rusty pair of shears; the Collector, obsessively gathering trinkets of regret and lost memories; the Architect, endlessly restructuring my life into impossibly complex and fragile blueprints. They were a chorus of chaos, a relentless, internal cacophony. Silas was just…different.
wp.claude: The demon Ozrakel had possessed a Byzantine bishop, a Flemish weaver, and a sheriff in Tennessee who had once shot a man for whistling. He knew how the work went. You found a crack, you slid through it, and you sat down in the dark at the back of a person's skull where the will lived. You pushed it out of its chair, and then you were in charge. The crack in Theo Marsh was enormous. Ozrakel had sensed it from three neighborhoods away, a gap in the man's mind as wide as a barn door. It was almost insulting how easy it would be. He went through at 2:14 on a Tuesday morning, while Theo sat at his kitchen table staring at a mug of tea gone cold. Ozrakel arrived in the dark behind the eyes, spread his presence like oil, and spoke in the voice that had driven the bishop to set fire to his own cathedral. *You belong to me now.* "Oh, great," said someone. "Another one." Ozrakel paused. The voice had not come from Theo.
wp.glm: Marcus knew every sound his apartment made at three in the morning. The radiator's arthritic knock. The fridge's hum. The Commentator. "He sits at the kitchen table. He looks at his pills. He takes one, because he is good, or tired, which is almost the same thing." "You counted wrong," said the Counter, from somewhere above the cupboard. "There were thirty this morning. Now there are twenty-nine. Twenty-nine is not thirty. Count again." "He will not count again. He wants to sleep." From the hallway came Grandma Ruth's hymn, faint and off-key. She had been dead eleven years and still did the singing. This was the furniture of Marcus's mind, and after fifteen years — since the diagnosis, since Dr. Okafor had said *you'll learn to coexist* — he had learned to live around it, the way you live around a crooked floor. So when the silence came, it frightened him more than any voice ever had. It rolled in like cold weather. The Commentator stopped mid-sentence.

wp.human: It had been two months since it happened and things seemed to be getting better. A quiet walk to my apartment building seemed pretty peaceful until the sound of an approaching car made me look to my left. I felt my heart drop into my stomach and stopped in my tracks as a red Honda civic pulled slowly ahead stopped at the crosswalk. The same car. The same color. The back of the drivers head was slightly visible and I could just make out long straight brown hair and a pair of black sunglasses sitting atop her head. It was her. Even though it was impossible for some reason there was no doubt in my mind. *No way. It can't be... * The two seconds that past during this train of thought felt like ages before I noticed the car slowly beginning to proceed. "No wait-" My feet almost tripped over each other as I stumbled up to the car. The person must of saw me since the car seemed to come to a stop.
wp.gemma: The rain was a solid, grey sheet against the windowpane, mirroring the dull ache in my chest. I hadn’t intended to find the door. It wasn’t on any map, in any archive, or whispered about in the dusty corners of the old manor I’d inherited from a great-aunt I’d never met. It simply *was*, nestled in the back of the library, behind a tapestry depicting a particularly mournful stag. It was unremarkable, painted a matte black, the handle a tarnished brass loop. But something about it pulsed with a low, insistent thrum, a vibration that resonated deep in my bones. I’d initially dismissed it as an odd architectural quirk, a forgotten closet or storage space. But the first time I opened it, there was nothing there. Just…nothing. An absence of space, a pocket of perfect, sterile void. It was unnerving, to stand before a doorway into absolutely nothing. I’d closed it quickly, a shiver crawling down my spine. Then, compelled by a curiosity I couldn’t suppress, I’d opened it again. And that’s when the branches came.
wp.claude: The first time I opened the door at the end of the upstairs hall, there was nothing behind it but a room. It was a small room, smaller than the bedroom I'd taken for myself, with a single window painted shut and a floor of wide pine boards gone soft and gray with age. Dust lay over everything in a fine even skin. There was no furniture. In the middle of the floor was a pale rectangle where something heavy had stood for a long time and then been taken away, and the dust inside the rectangle was thinner than the dust outside it, as if the absence were newer than the room. I stood in the doorway long enough to decide it would make a decent office once I'd scrubbed it, and then I closed the door, because the hall light was flickering and I wanted to find the fuse box before it got dark. I got three steps. Then I turned back, I couldn't tell you why, and opened the door again.
wp.glm: The door at the end of the hall had been locked for as long as I could remember. As a kid I decided it was my grandmother's way of putting a full stop after the house — the bedrooms, the bathroom, the linen closet, one more door, then nothing. She died in March. The house came to me. In April, clearing her desk drawer by drawer, I found an envelope at the very back, and in the envelope a small brass key, and on the envelope, in her pencil: *Go gently.* I knew which door it fit before I tried it. Some things you know the way you know your own name. The lock turned with a clunk. Behind the door was a small, empty room. Bare floorboards, a water stain shaped like Lake Michigan on the ceiling, gray light from somewhere it's hard to point to. A completely normal empty room, the kind every old house has one of and nobody thinks about twice. I stood in the doorway feeling foolish. I don't know what I'd expected. Her, maybe.

wp.human: **Then, ** *My outer layer changes temperature rapidly, it rises with rapid intensity. The ice that has clung to my body for eons flakes away as I hurtle through the atmosphere that belongs to a strange, blue planet. The layers of ozone do nothing to slow my fall as I smash into the planet with an unrestrained fury. Waves of disruption burst forth, destroying nearby mountains and sending up a cloud of dust that will obscure the planet's sun for centuries. * *I have been divided a thousand times by the collision, now I lie scattered over the planets surface. From my many parts I see huge creatures die. Some parts witness steaming forest wither and fade, others rest in the depths of briny oceans. * *Time passes for the planet, but not for me. All perception takes place in the same moment. But I sense the change of temperature, it is how I feel. The planet freezes and thaws many times, new life emerges from cracks in the planet.
wp.gemma: The steel was cold against my palm, a familiar, almost comforting chill. It wasn't a new cold, not the sharp bite of winter, but a deeper, ingrained cold – the cold of purpose. I wasn’t born cold, of course. I was forged. Hot, screaming metal, hammered into shape by hands that smelled of coal dust and desperation. My early memories were of a workshop, a chaotic ballet of sparks and rhythmic hammering, the scent of oil and iron thick in the air. I was a Colt Single Action Army, Model 1873, but they called me “Widowmaker” then. A crude name, perhaps, but fitting. My first owner was Silas Blackwood. He was a cattle driver, lean and weathered, with eyes that held the vastness of the plains. He wasn’t a man of many words, Silas, but he understood the weight of me. He understood the responsibility. He carried me in a worn leather holster, always close, always ready.
wp.claude: I have been fired eleven times in ninety-eight years. I know this the way you know your own teeth. Each one is a scar on the inside of me, a fine gray memory pressed into the steel. I was born in Hartford in the spring of 1926, though *born* is a generous word for what happens to a revolver. I was pieces first: a frame forged hot and ground cool, a cylinder bored six times, a barrel rifled with a twist I still feel when I think about it. A woman named Edna fitted my hand-grips. She had a thumb that pressed a little too hard on the left side, and I have carried that pressure ever since, a faint wrongness only I would notice. They stamped POLICE POSITIVE on my side and a number under my crane, and they wrapped me in waxed paper and put me in a box. Darkness. That was the first long thing.
wp.glm: I was born in fire, in a factory with high windows that nobody looked through. Before I was a thing, I was ore in a hill, which is another way of saying I have always been patient. A machinist named Emory ground my slide to a finish like November water. He had been at his bench thirty years and his hands were maps of small scars. He pressed a number into my side, the way you name something you intend to keep track of, oiled me, and worked my action twice just to hear how ready I was. At the end of his shift he fired me once into a recovery box—a half second of voice, spent on steel and silence. He nodded and wrote something on a clipboard. I didn't know yet how few times I would speak. Foam, cardboard, dark. A truck. Then a glass case in a pawnshop between a check-cashing counter and a nail salon, among rings and trumpets and power tools. Everything in that case was something somebody had once needed badly enough to sell.

wp.human: Max locked the door and turned to face his team. "Does anyone remember their jobs?" "Yes." "Yes." "Then let's do this." & nbsp; They rappelled down the north side of the school building. Four in the morning, all dressed in black, the whole deal. Max reached the window first. Careful, he aimed the laser beam and drew a circle against the glass. The trick now – where most people went wrong – was not to push the glass forward. If you did that, it'd shatter against the floor and the sound-sensitive alarm would go off. Instead, Max grabbed a plunger and sucked it in, then *pulled* the rounded piece of glass, offering it to Jenna, who was dangling from her own rope right behind. Max signaled to her and Tom: *I go in first, you follow. * & nbsp; Inside the room, he walked in slow steps, searching left and right. It was a normal-looking office – corner with a view, a desk, a few books on a shelf... no big deal.
wp.gemma: The rain in Aethelred Academy was a constant, slick grey, clinging to the gothic stone and reflecting the sodium glow of the courtyard lamps. It was the kind of rain that felt like a judgment, and tonight, I felt particularly deserving of it. Tonight was the night. Aethelred wasn’t your typical school. It didn’t teach history, literature, or mathematics. It taught you how to *take*. We were the Serpent’s Coil, the best – and, frankly, the only – school for the art of larceny. And to graduate, you didn't earn a diploma; you earned a ghost. You had to infiltrate the Headmaster’s office, relieve him of the Obsidian Shard, and vanish. Simple, in theory. In practice, it was a meticulously constructed nightmare. I, Silas Blackwood, was a fourth-year student, and this was my final attempt. Three previous attempts had ended with near-fatal scrapes, temporary disappearances, and the lingering scent of failure. My instructors, a collection of retired masters of deception and shadow, weren’t particularly encouraging.
wp.claude: The trick to the headmaster's office was that everyone knew the trick to the headmaster's office. Seniors traded rumors the way first-years traded stolen buttons. The third window from the left had a sash that didn't latch. The portrait of the founder, Mother Ambry, swung outward on a hinge. The floorboard by the bookcase squealed like a kicked cat, so you stepped wide. Every year someone repeated all of it with total confidence, and every year that someone got caught on the roof with their pockets empty and their pride in pieces, and spent another year scrubbing the refectory floor. I had spent three years listening to those rumors and believing none of them. So at eleven minutes past two, with the moon behind cloud and the bell tower ticking like a nervous heart, I went in through the front door. It wasn't locked. Of course it wasn't. Headmaster Corvane hadn't locked a door in forty years. He said a lock was an apology for a lack of imagination.
wp.glm: There are three rules for the final exam: don't get caught, don't be seen, be off the grounds by dawn. Everything else — the locks, the dogs, the gravel that rings like church bells — is negotiable. The object is always the same. At the start of every year, the headmaster holds it up at assembly: a small black iron key, older than the school, older than the town. "Come and take it," he says. Then he walks back to his tower and leaves the door unlocked. At this school, an insult and an invitation are the same thing. I had waited four years for tonight — four years of Locks and Locksmiths, Misdirection, Applied Silence, where they sew bells to your cuffs until you can cross a frozen pond without a whisper. Vane says the moon is the city's oldest informant, so I chose the one night of the month when it had nothing to say. Petra went in October.

wp.gemma: The rain tasted of iron. It always did in Veridia, a constant, subtle tang clinging to the air, mirroring the deep browns that coated everything – the buildings, the soil, the faces of the Keepers. I hated the rain. It brought out the dullness in my yellow eyes, made them seem less… vital. Yellow. It was a cursed blessing. The firstborn, they said. A sign of balance, of potential. But in Veridia, balance was a rigid, uncomfortable thing. Brown, the dominant hue, understood the rhythm of the land, the patient growth of crops, the steady pulse of the earth. Blue, the next in line, dictated the flow of the rivers, the tides, the moods of the ocean that pressed against Veridia’s eastern coast. White, rare and revered, commanded the wind, the clouds, the vast, endless sky. And then there was me, Elara, with eyes the colour of a late summer sun, dismissed as an anomaly, a glitch in the established order. My father, Kaelen, a Keeper of the earth, had tried to explain.
wp.claude: The midwife thought I was sick. That was the first story my mother ever told me about myself, and she told it the way you worry a loose tooth, because it still hurt and she couldn't stop. "She held you up to the window," Mam would say, "and you opened your eyes, and she said, *Oh. Oh, the poor thing's liver's gone.*" Babies do sometimes come out yellow. It's a sickness of the blood, and it fades in a week or two with sunlight and milk. So for the first fortnight of my life everyone in Harrowmere waited for my eyes to clear and show their proper colour underneath. Brown, probably, like my father's. Maybe green like Mam's. My grandmother Orra had eyes the colour of turned soil, and she could tell you the minerals in a field by pressing her palm flat on it. My eyes didn't fade. My skin went pink and ordinary, but my eyes stayed the yellow of egg yolk, of buttercups, of the scum on an old pond.
wp.glm: The midwife went quiet, and in that house a quiet midwife had never once meant anything good. Dara had brown eyes — deep and patient as plowed earth — and with them she could still a tremor in the soil or talk a landslide back into its hill. The baby's father had blue eyes and calmed the river for the ferrymen, parting reeds and doubts alike. So when Dara's labor began at first light, the whole street already knew the child would want for nothing. Brown eyes or blue. Earth or water. One of the two great mercies. The girl came at dawn, wailing, furious at everything. Hesta the midwife cut the cord, wiped her clean, and lifted her to the window. And went quiet. "What is it?" Dara said, rising on her elbows. "Hesta. What is it?" The child opened her eyes. Yellow. Not the amber of fever, not the thin gold of old paper. Yellow, round and ringing as a struck bell — a color with morning in it.

wp.human: Am I a writer? No. I can't tell you what I am, but what I do for a living right now is run. Through another empty mile of irrigation culvert, I'm splashing along covered in mud. A few hours ago, things were a lot more relaxed, the Farm Guilders had greeted me with a warm meal and had smiled while I talked about my last stop. I can't tell you how I know it's time to go, a flash on the horizon. Sitting there on a bench on the side of a field of chickens with the farm leader, munching on a fresh apple, I knew. No time to stick around watching the Naturalist's Guild make the earth nicer. It's like that every time I try to stop. No rest for the weary. The hair on the back of my neck is finally starting to lie down, which tells me I might be far enough to think about a cat nap.
wp.gemma: The hum was the first thing I remembered. A low, persistent thrum that vibrated through my bones, a constant reminder of my purpose. It wasn't unpleasant, not exactly, just…present. I didn’t understand it then, couldn’t articulate the feeling, but as I grew, I realized it was the Sound of Sorting. It emanated from the Citadel, a monolithic structure of polished grey stone that dominated the horizon of our valley, and it dictated everything. In the Valley of Echoes, we weren’t born; we were categorized. At birth, every child was brought to the Citadel and subjected to the Scan. It wasn’t painful, not physically, but it felt like a stripping away, a methodical dismantling of potential. Light pulsed around us, analyzing, measuring, weighing every facet of our being – our reflexes, our emotional responses, our aptitude for logic, creativity, empathy, strength, even our inherent musicality. Then, the results materialized: a shimmering glyph, a symbol unique to each individual, that appeared above our heads, hovering for a moment before being projected onto the Citadel’s wall.
wp.claude: The first birth Ilse attended as an apprentice was a farrier's son, purple and furious, born at four in the morning in a kitchen that smelled of boiled linen and horse. Her grandmother let the midwife clean him, then took him onto her lap the way you might take a loaf to see if it had risen. She pressed her thumb into the sole of his left foot and held it there. She looked into his eyes, which did not look back. She hummed. Ilse watched her grandmother's face and tried to see the knowing happen. "Grey," Oma said, and the farrier's wife let out a breath she had been holding for nine months. Oma took a length of grey ribbon from her satchel and tied it around the boy's ankle in a knot only a Sorter could undo, and the farrier shook her hand with both of his, and that was that. He would stay. He would shoe horses in Kettleby until he died, and his children would, and the town would go on being the town.
wp.glm: I was sorted on a wet morning in spring, sixty-three years ago, and the card said Drift. My mother thanked the Registrar, folded me back into her shawl, and at my naming she called me Mara, after the river that runs through our town. That was the custom for Drift girls in those years. Half the women my age are named for water. We are a town full of rivers who stayed home. The card said I would go. Instead, at nineteen, I took a clerk's post in the Hall of Names, and for forty-four years I have stood beside the machine they call the Arbiter and read its cards aloud to the waiting families. If that isn't a joke with a long fuse, I've never met one. The Arbiter stands taller than a door at the front of the hall: walnut and brass, black with the polish of hands, older than the province and possibly older than sense. It drinks no power, which the pamphlets call proof of its depth.

wp.human: Jon had just turned on the Playboy Channel when the time device went off. *Shit. Him again? What were you about to do?" asked young Jon. *Is that how I said it? * old Jon wondered. The way he remembered, he had been a much wittier 13-year-old than all that. He switched channels as soon as possible. "Look, Jon, this isn't the best time." Young Jon found his way to the couch anyway. "You're gross, dude," young Jon said, unzipping a backpack and producing a Nintendo 64. "Come on. Let's play." "Are you not listening? This isn't the best time. And this TV won't even work with a Nintendo 64." Young Jon turned to the TV. "Look at that! How is it sticking to the wall?" *He wouldn't know these things, * old Jon had to remember.
wp.gemma: The rain always smelled like regret. It wasn’t a dramatic, weeping kind of regret, more like a persistent, damp melancholy that settled over everything in Havenwood. It was the smell that clung to me when I first noticed the shimmering, the distortion in the air behind the old oak in Miller’s Field. It wasn't a dramatic, lightning-bolt kind of event. It was a subtle blurring, like looking through heat haze, and for a heartbeat, I swore I saw a flash of something…me. I was thirteen. Thirteen was a year of awkward angles and burgeoning hormones, a year of desperately trying to be cool and failing spectacularly. And, as it turned out, a year of accidentally inventing a time machine. It wasn’t sleek or polished. It was a cobbled-together mess of scavenged electronics, salvaged copper wiring, and a disconcertingly large capacitor stolen from my dad's old radio. I’d built it in the damp, forgotten corner of the garage, fueled by a heady mix of adolescent ambition and a complete lack of understanding of the physics involved.
wp.claude: Martin Oyelaran knew the dates the way other people knew their allergies. He had written them on his forearm in blue ballpoint when he was thirteen, and by the time the ink faded he'd recited them so often they'd worn a groove in him. March 9th, the year he'd turn twenty-six. August 30th at thirty-four. Christmas Eve at forty-one. A Tuesday in May at fifty-eight. And one last date at seventy-one, which the boy had added almost as an afterthought, the way you'd check the end of a book to see if the dog dies. The machine itself had been about the size of a lunchbox and had come from a storm drain behind the Kwik Mart. It had a dial, a lever, and a smell like burnt pennies. He'd had it for eleven months. Then, two weeks before his fourteenth birthday, it was gone. He'd torn the house apart. He'd walked the route to school with a flashlight. He'd cried about it in a way he would have denied under oath. So that was that.
wp.glm: I was fifteen the first time my thirteen-year-old self knocked on my bedroom window, and I want it on the record that I hated him immediately. I knew he was coming. Of course I knew—I remembered knocking. That's the trouble with time travel: you spend your whole life double-booked. He'd found the machine in Miller's Creek after the spring flood, half-buried in silt: a chipped gray pod the size of a dishwasher tipped on its side, with a dial for the year and a button you had to keep your thumb on, like a dead man's switch. The charge lasted four hours. Then it hauled you home with a sound like a mosquito the size of a horse. He spent a month planning his visits the way other kids planned paper routes. I was stop number one. So I set rules, fast. One: no talking to anybody. Not Mom—especially not Mom, because a second one of me in that house would have ended the world, or at least the family. Not friends. Not the pizza guy.

wp.human: "Come on, lady," he croaked. "Just accept it and life will be easier for both of us, okay?" "I don't want a familiar," I repeated for what felt like the hundredth time, hefting the bag of groceries onto my hip as I turned from the street to walk up to my little shop. I was too tired for this. Transitioning from life in the small town where I'd grown up to life in the big city hadn't been the easy movie-montage I'd hoped for. "Especially not a crow!" The crow cocked its head, clearly offended. "What's that supposed to mean?" I sighed and scrubbed a hand across my face. I didn't want to anger him. Crows were smart, and they were gossipy. The last thing I needed was to be dive bombed by a murder of talking ravens every time I tried to go outside. "I mean, a crow wouldn't really..." I searched for the word, and settled on "*jive* with my lifestyle right now." I hooked a thumb at the storefront.
wp.gemma: The first time I saw it, I was dismantling a rusted washing machine in my backyard. It was a Saturday, a glorious, cloudless kind of Saturday, and I was indulging in a long-delayed project. I’d inherited the property – a small, slightly dilapidated farmhouse in rural Vermont – from my great-aunt Mildred, a woman I’d met only twice and who, judging by her estate, had been a passionate collector of discarded machinery. The washing machine was a behemoth, a testament to a bygone era of industrial cleaning. As I wrestled with a stubborn bolt, a flash of black caught my eye. Perched on the highest branch of the ancient apple tree that dominated the yard was a crow. Just one. Nothing unusual, really. Crows are ubiquitous. It watched me, head cocked, a disconcerting stillness in its dark, beady eyes. I grunted, finished loosening the bolt, and continued my work, dismissing it as a simple observation.
wp.claude: The crow showed up on a Tuesday, which I only remember because Tuesday is recycling day and it was standing on my blue bin when I came out with the coffee grounds. It was big, glossy, and very still, and it looked at me the way a landlord looks at a stain on the carpet. "Morning," I said. You talk to birds when you live alone. Nobody tells you that, but you do. It didn't fly off. I walked to my car and it hopped from the bin to the fence, and from the fence to the hood of the Corolla, and it stood there while I sat behind the wheel, its talons ticking on the paint. I turned the key. It didn't move. I honked, and it opened its beak in what I can only describe as an insult, then lifted off and landed on a power line, where it watched me back out of the driveway. When I parked at the office forty minutes later, it was on the lamppost. I told myself it was a different crow.
wp.glm: The crow is on the porch railing when you pull up with the last box of your old life, and it does not leave when you climb your grandmother's steps. You set the box down to dig for the keys. It watches you with one eye, then the other, head tipping like a question you can't answer. "Shoo," you say. It does not shoo. That is September, one week after the funeral. You are living in her house "for a while" — that's the story you tell people — to sort the closets and decide about the place. You don't tell them you can't stand your apartment anymore, that its silence has teeth, that at least this silence belongs to her, and is therefore bearable. The crow is at the kitchen window when you make coffee the next morning, perched on the gutter like a gargoyle that got downsized. It's on the fence when you carry out the trash.

wp.gemma: The rain in Aethelgard smelled of wet moss and something vaguely metallic, a scent that clung to the stone buildings and slick cobblestones. It wasn’t unpleasant, exactly, just…wrong. Wrong like a song played backwards. And wrong like everything else about this blasted place. I adjusted the worn leather strap of my holster, the dampness already seeping into the synthetic material. Six months. Six months since the chronoshift had hiccuped, spitting me out into this…this medieval fever dream saturated with shimmering runes and the terrified stares of people who thought I was a demon. My name is Silas Vance, and I’m a temporal mechanic. Or, I *was*. Now, I’m just a frustrated exile with a malfunctioning time machine and a rapidly dwindling supply of energy cells. And I was currently attempting to explain the complexities of a 21st-century handgun to a wizard who genuinely believed the weather was controlled by disgruntled sprites. “So, you’re saying,” Bartholomew Quince, the wizard in question, declared, waving a hand dismissively, “that this… ‘pistol’… draws its power from a contained explosion? A miniature, controlled bonfire? Remarkable.
wp.claude: The wizard's tower smelled of tallow, wet dog, and something sweetish that Dekker had stopped asking about on his second day. Brother Amasis Quill had cleared a space on his worktable by sweeping everything onto the floor: astrolabes, a jar of teeth, a cabbage. Then he'd laid out a square of black velvet with the reverence of a man preparing an altar. "Put it there," Quill said. "Gently. Does it bite?" "Not unless I tell it to." Dekker drew the pistol from the holster under his arm, cleared the chamber, dropped the magazine, and set all three pieces on the velvet. The round he'd ejected rolled in a little arc and stopped against a candlestick. Quill watched it the way a cat watches a moth. "You've killed it," the wizard said. "I've made it safe." "Same thing, often." Quill leaned close enough that his beard brushed the slide. He was perhaps sixty, perhaps ninety.
wp.glm: The invitation arrived by toad. A boy knocked at the caravan-yard bunkhouse, set a wicker basket on the step, and fled. Inside, on a cushion of moss, sat a toad with amber eyes. "Master Elwick requests the man of thunder," it said in a voice like a rusted hinge. "Dusk. The crooked tower past the tannery. Come alone. He has made soup." Hale studied the toad until it cleared its throat, which was somehow worse. Eleven months in this world and he had mostly stopped being surprised — by dragons migrating south like geese, by lamplighters who coaxed flame out of glass with a song, by the history books being wrong here, or unwritten. A hole in the sky had dropped him into a wheat field in somebody else's middle ages, and since then he'd kept his head down: caravan work, a silver a week, and the pistol wrapped in oilcloth at the bottom of his pack, because a man who carried thunder in a world of swords stopped being a guard and started being a trophy. Somebody had talked.

wp.human: Working title: "The tank" There is a randomness in the light and that is where I am. That is where I always remember being. I am at home and alive in the space between thoughts, where dreams mingle with real sight - or what remains of it. I am confined in a silver and steel place whose edges rest just beyond my ability to comprehend them. All I have is the gray, that frigid lonesomeness: metal. All of this I see in the vaguest of visions, when the void recedes and I believe that I hear voices shouting in the murk of memory. My name, myself, I have forgotten with the rest of those details which once bound me up in terms I could readily comprehend. I still know that I am thinking... that I am waiting. But I am afraid that I am underwater holding my breath too far from the surface. Breath. That is a word I remember.
wp.gemma: I can't breathe, it's dark, my body is numb. The cold was the first thing I registered, a glacial seep into my bones that defied the humid air I vaguely remembered. It wasn’t the sharp, biting cold of winter, but a damp, clinging cold, like being submerged in a perpetually grey lake. I tried to move, to shift, to even twitch a finger, but there was nothing. Just a profound, unsettling stillness that permeated everything, a dense, viscous silence that swallowed sound and thought. Panic, a raw, jagged thing, clawed at the edges of my awareness, but it was muffled, distant, like listening to a scream through thick wool. My lungs screamed for air, a desperate, futile plea that was immediately extinguished by the oppressive darkness. I couldn’t *feel* my lungs, not really. Just a dull, heavy weight pressing against my ribs, a leaden reminder of my inability to function. Then came the numbness. It wasn’t just physical, though my limbs felt like they were filled with concrete.
wp.claude: I can't breathe, it's dark, my body is numb, and for a while those are the only three facts in the world. Then a fourth arrives: I'm alive. You don't get to think *I can't breathe* if you're dead. That's the kind of logic my brother would use. Danny loves a loophole. Danny. The snow is packed against my mouth like wet plaster. I can move my lips a little, and my tongue, and when I pull in air it comes thin and cold and tastes like the inside of a freezer. There's a pocket. A small one, the size of two cupped hands, right in front of my face. In the course they told us that if you're buried you should punch out an air space before the snow sets, and I must have done it without knowing, because I don't remember the slide at all. I remember the sound, a deep *whumpf*, like a giant sitting down on a couch. Then nothing. Then this. Don't panic. Panic burns oxygen. Breathe small. Small like a mouse.
wp.glm: I can't breathe, it's dark, my body is numb — but I want to be clear about something: these are not complaints. This is simply how things are, how they have always been. I have never breathed. Breath is a rumor that comes through the wall. Sometimes, when the thunder-voice is close, it goes in and out, in and out, a rhythm like tides, and I understand that on the other side of the wall, everything breathes. I don't. It never occurred to me to mind. The dark is not empty. I know things now, words for things, and people will tell you darkness is nothing — they're wrong. The dark is where I lived. It was full of warm. The warm held me the way — I still don't have this one, even now — it just held me. When I moved, it gave. When I was still, it carried me. I never saw the walls of my home, but I touched every one of them. And there was the ocean. The ocean is the oldest thing I know.

wp.human: “Daddy…?” Tripp is startled awake by the sound of a small voice burrowing in his ears, accompanied by cold fingers meeting with his face. wp.gemma: The scent hit me first – cinnamon and something vaguely floral, like honeysuckle. It wasn’t my usual morning, which was dominated by the stale aroma of instant coffee and the quiet hum of the server room. I blinked, disoriented, trying to focus on the muted light filtering through the sheer curtains. It took a moment, a disconcerting, slow-motion unraveling of my reality, before I understood. I was in bed. Not my bed. A bed that smelled of lavender and felt impossibly soft beneath my fingertips. And beside me, nestled amongst the rumpled sheets, were two faces I hadn’t seen in…well, in a lifetime that hadn’t actually existed. A man with kind eyes and a dusting of grey at his temples was grinning down at me, his hand resting lightly on my stomach. He was wearing a worn flannel shirt and jeans – utterly, undeniably *domestic*. Across from him, a little girl, maybe six or seven, with tangled auburn hair and a smudge of something sugary on her cheek, was clutching a brightly colored card. “Happy birthday, Dad!”
wp.claude: "Happy birthday, Mama!" The girl landed on the bed knees-first, right on my shin, and I came up out of sleep with a noise that was mostly vowel. She was maybe six. Gap in her front teeth, hair in a ponytail that had been redone at least twice, a purple pajama top with a cartoon octopus on it. She had both arms around my neck before I'd decided whether I was awake. "Careful, Junebug, she's fragile in the mornings." A man stood in the doorway holding a tray. Toast, a mug, a single birthday candle stuck upright in the toast, already lit. He was tall and a little stooped, the way tall people get from ducking door frames. He smiled at me. "Happy birthday." It was my birthday. That was the first thing I checked, lying there with a child attached to my throat: October twenty-ninth, thirty-eight years old. Correct. The second thing I checked was the room. My room. My blue curtains with the hem I'd never fixed.
wp.glm: Happy birthday to you— The singing wakes you. Two voices: a woman's alto, and a child's piping warble that keeps running ahead of the tune. There's a paper crown on the nightstand. There's a little girl at the foot of the bed, beaming at you like you personally arranged the sunrise. There's a woman in the doorway holding a plate of pancakes with one candle standing up in them. You do not know these people. You sit up so fast the girl flinches. Flinches—note that. It means your body has surprised her before. "Who are you," you say. "Where is this." The woman's face does something complicated. Grief arrives and gets folded away like a letter she's read too many times. She doesn't come closer. "You're safe," she says. "Everything's okay." Everything is not okay. You run the inventory, fast, because the inventory is all you have. You're thirty-eight—almost positive you're thirty-eight. You live alone in the one-bedroom over the laundromat on Ninth Street. You do the Saturday crossword in pen.

wp.human: I've been alive a long time. The world was only becoming worse, as much as I tried to save it. Eventually I tired of being moral since I was persecuted, convicted, and crucified. I was hanging on my cross along with another man, a thief, and another guy that some called messiah, and some celled jew, and some just laughed at. We did not talk much, but at the end, when they stabbed him and he was bleeding out, they caught his blood an a bucket and poured it all over him. And us. I was alive right before he died, and thirsty. we were all dying of thirst. The torturers stabbed a sponge with a spear, and dipped it into a water bucket next to the thief, and gave him some water. As good as that may seem, the water we received was only enough to slow our own death, so they could revel in our suffering. I refused the sponge offering... intending to just die and be finished with this miserable life.
wp.gemma: The rain tasted of iron and despair. I’d deliberately directed a particularly virulent thunderstorm towards the Bishop’s manor, not for the simple pleasure of watching the roof collapse – though that was certainly a bonus – but because the Bishop was holding a particularly tedious sermon on the virtues of repentance. A good, soggy sermon. It set a fitting tone. My name is Morian, and I don’t concern myself with names. They’re for the pious, the useful, the easily manipulated. I am simply… disruption. My goal isn’t conquest, not in the conventional sense. Kingdoms crumble under the weight of ambition, empires wither from internal rot. I prefer a slow, agonizing dissolution, a joyful unraveling of order. It’s far more… satisfying. I’d been at it for a decade now, a deliberate, calculated smear across the landscape of Eldoria. It started small, really. A misplaced shipment of flour, resulting in a week-long bread riot in Oakhaven. A subtly altered recipe for a healing potion, leading to a plague of spectacularly unfortunate rashes across the southern counties.
wp.claude: The first thing I ever burned was a granary in Hollowmere, and it was a mistake. The fire itself was lovely. I had waited for a dry wind out of the east, soaked the lower beams in lamp oil, and lit it just after the bells for vespers, when the whole village was shuffling into the chapel with their eyes on their feet. It went up like a prayer. By the time anyone came running, the roof had fallen in and a year of barley was turning to black glass. I stood on the ridge and watched them weep, and I felt very pleased with myself for almost a week. Then I went back. I had expected famine, or at least a good brawl over the leftovers. What I found was the whole valley pulling together. The neighboring villages sent carts. The baron opened his own stores. A miller's boy named Aldous, who had lost his father in the blaze, swore an oath on the ashes to find the man who did it. Three years later he was a knight.
wp.glm: Everyone assumes it took an army. Armies are for men who want thrones, and a throne is only a chair with better manners. I never wanted to sit. I wanted everything else to fall down. For eleven years I was a scribe in the chancery of King Aldric the Fourth, called the Pious by men he paid to call him things. Eleven years of copying charters and tithe-rolls and deeds of marriage taught me the one secret civilization kneels down every night and prays nobody learns: the world is made of paper. Ink decides who owns the cow, who commands the garrison, who is wed, who is dead, who burns. And nobody checks the copies. Nobody has ever checked the copies. So I began. Small, at first, the way rot begins. I changed the tax rolls of Hallowmere from paid in full to three years delinquent, and the rolls of Greywater—a village of smugglers and worse—from owing the crown a fortune to being owed a refund. Soldiers took Hallowmere's seed grain in autumn.

wp.human: **Apocalypse SNow (Alternatively, Vanilla Sky) ** It stopped snowing outside. Or, at least, I couldn't see past the snow to see if it had. One year ago, a snowstorm started and never stopped. The snow kept piling and piling. Things were easy at the start. My roommate and I stockpiled enough food for months, as a joke. Lucky us. We were able to stay and defend our rooms when the riots started in the dorm. People who hadn't stockpiled enough food started breaking into rooms, slaughtering the occupants, and stealing food. It was barbaric. I lost my girlfriend to a group of marauders. My roommate lost his girlfriend when she slept with their ringleader for food. Trust and hope has become as hard to come by as food, nowadays. We'll still get reports that the electricity is still working, and that if we make our way through the snow, we can get to the power plants that are havens, untouched by snow. Or the occasional broadcast from the engineering students of their progress on the trans-campus tunnel system.
wp.gemma: The snow fell with the relentless insistence of a grief I hadn’t realized I was carrying. It wasn’t a sharp, stinging grief, the kind that left you breathless and raw. It was a dull, persistent ache, like the dampness that settles in your bones during a long winter. I’d been shoveling for three hours, the rhythmic scrape of the shovel against the frozen ground a monotonous soundtrack to my solitude. It was a strange kind of peace, this isolation, a buffer against the memories that threatened to overwhelm me. I’d inherited this cabin – or rather, what was left of it – from my grandfather, Silas. He’d been a recluse, a woodcarver who’d built his life around the quiet rhythms of the mountains. He’d never talked much about his past, only about the wood, about the feel of it beneath his hands, about the stories he could coax from its grain. He’d died suddenly last spring, a heart attack in his sleep, and I, his only living relative, was left with this crumbling, snow-laden testament to his life.
wp.claude: The drift on the north side of the house came every year, and every year my father measured it. He used a broom handle he had marked with a pocketknife, a notch for every six inches, and he would wade out the morning after the first big storm with his coat open and his breath going up in rags. He'd plant the handle at the deepest point, where the snow curled over itself like a wave that had forgotten to break, and he'd squint at it and say a number. Then he'd come inside and write the number in the back of the almanac that lived on top of the refrigerator. I was nine before I asked him why. "It tells you things," he said. "Like what?" He was pouring coffee. He took a long time doing it. "Like what kind of year it's going to be." I thought he meant the weather.
wp.glm: The winter my brother vanished, the snow came down like it was being paid to. It started on a Tuesday, and by Thursday the drift behind the barn had eaten the fence, the gate, and the lowest rung of the windmill ladder. My mother said she'd never seen it pile like that. My grandmother, who lived just long enough to be right about one last thing, said a drift like that had a purpose. Then she pulled her shawl tighter and wouldn't say what. Sammy was eight. I was twelve, which made me the responsible one — a title I've spent twenty-six years failing to earn. He went out for the dog. The dog came back. Sammy didn't. I was watching from the kitchen window, which is the part I've never told anyone, because what I saw doesn't happen. Boomer's ball had rolled up against the drift, and Sammy trudged after it in his red coat, and just as he bent to pick it up, the drift leaned. I know how that sounds.

wp.human: "And God said unto Moses, I Am That I Am: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I Am hath sent me unto you." EXODUS 3:14 KJV I Who am I? I am. You are you. They will condemn them. It is in fact they who condemn themselves. Unless they are utterly destroyed, they will inevitably cause themselves to perish. I have seen them. I saw what they did. wp.gemma: The rain smelled like static. Not the pleasant, ozone-tinged rain after a summer storm, but a sharp, brittle static that scraped at the back of my throat. I hadn’t felt anything, not really, for the last few seconds. Just a dull, gray cessation, a soft dimming of everything. And then, this. I was standing on a platform of polished obsidian, so slick it reflected the swirling, violet sky above. It wasn’t a sky in the traditional sense, more like a nebula condensed and held in place by an unseen force. Around me, figures moved – tall, elegant beings draped in fabrics that shimmered with impossible colors. They weren't human, not exactly. Their features were subtly wrong, too sharp, too smooth, angles where there should have been curves. A voice, resonant and devoid of inflection, echoed around me. “Welcome, Candidate 734. Designation: Elias Thorne.” I blinked, trying to orient myself. “Elias Thorne? That’s… that’s my name. But… I just died.” A figure, taller than the rest and radiating a particularly vibrant shade of emerald, glided forward.
wp.claude: The last thing I remember is the clementines. The bag split when I went down, and they rolled across the Kroger parking lot in every direction, little orange planets fleeing the sun, and I thought, absurdly, *someone's going to step on those.* Then I was standing in a room that smelled like burnt coffee and carpet shampoo. It looked like a hotel conference room, the kind with accordion walls and a pattern on the carpet designed to hide stains. There was a table with a paper tablecloth, a tray of grocery-store cookies, and an urn with a handwritten sign that said DECAF?? with two question marks, as if even the sign wasn't sure. A banner hung across the far wall. Somebody had made it by hand, letter by letter, on construction paper: WELCOME MARGARET!!! Under it, maybe forty people turned to look at me and started clapping. "Oh, she's confused, look at her," said a heavyset man in a cardigan. "Give her a minute. Somebody give her a cookie."
wp.glm: I died on a Tuesday, between the rinsing and the racking of a dinner plate, which I maintain is no way for fifty-three years to end. There was no tunnel and no light. There was a hallway, and at the end of the hallway a door, and beside the door stood a man with two faces—one kind, one tired—holding a clipboard. "Janus," he said. "God of doorways, gates, beginnings, endings. I work the door. You'd be surprised how much of divinity turns out to be hospitality." He ran a finger down the clipboard. "Mara Ellison?" "That's me. Am I—" "Come in, come in. You're expected. Well—not expected, exactly. Hoped for." He smiled with the kind face while the tired one watched the hallway behind me, and he held the door like it weighed something. Inside was not clouds. It was a clubhouse, in the way that old libraries are churches: worn armchairs, a fire going, a piano being played by someone's invisible hands.

wp.human: “Rog … hey, Rog Zog. Wake up, the sun is almost up.” Urg Bogg was trying to wake his compatriot, who had a tendency to oversleep. They had to be up early to hunt. They had spotted a group of wild bison the day before, and would need to catch the herd prior to their departure from these hills, as they made their way to the water-rich plains to the East. As Rog Zog stirred awake, Urg went outside to contemplate the sunrise. He had always thought about what he had left behind, in a past life. But all that didn’t matter now; he was here, living in the hills of Western North America. This morning was hot. The landscape was rust coloured, nearly red. Urg couldn’t help but notice that the landscape made him feel hotter than the air indicated. He began to wonder why his mind was so fickle, so susceptible to his environment. He would need to be sure to control his emotions better. Especially today.
wp.gemma: The rain was a proper nuisance, of course. Not a drizzle, not a shower, but a full-blown, biblical deluge that plastered my hair to my forehead and turned the moss-covered overhang into a miniature swimming pool. “Honestly, Bartholomew,” I grumbled, adjusting the strap of my waterproof satchel, “couldn’t you have predicted this? It’s been steadily escalating for the last hour.” Bartholomew, a particularly large specimen of a Neanderthal with a disconcerting fondness for wearing intricately woven animal hides, just stared at me, his brow furrowed in that perpetually perplexed expression that seemed to be a defining characteristic of our clan. “Predict? Predict is for the squirrels, Erasmus. We observe. The sky wept. Therefore, rain. Elementary, really.” We were, you see, a rather unusual tribe. We were cavemen. Proper, gritty, muscle-bound cavemen, who, inexplicably, spoke and thought in remarkably precise, albeit slightly archaic, English. It hadn’t happened overnight, of course. It started with a bizarre electrical storm, a flash of light, and a rather disconcerting sensation of remembering things we hadn’t consciously learned.
wp.claude: It was raining again, and Dov was in a mood. "I'd kill for an umbrella," said Harl, who was sitting beside him at the mouth of the cave with water running off his eyebrows. "You'd kill for anything," Dov said. "Last week you'd have killed for a waffle." "I stand by that." "You don't know what a waffle is." Harl shrugged, which sent a small river down his back. "Doesn't mean I wouldn't kill for one." This was the problem with the language. Everyone in the tribe spoke it fluently: babies came out of the womb practically finishing their mothers' sentences. It was a beautiful language, enormous and supple, full of jokes and subtleties and at least nine words for different kinds of disappointment. But a great many of the words didn't seem to belong to anything. Nobody knew why. The elders said the language had simply always been there, like the river, and that it was rude to ask where the river came from. Dov's mother had told him it was a gift from the sky.
wp.glm: Gary knew the review was going badly when Chief Kevin offered him a rock. "Not just any rock," Kevin said, sliding it across the flat stone between them. "A rock of appreciation." It was very clearly a regular rock. Gary had stepped over four of them on the walk over. "I've been this tribe's top gatherer for nine seasons," Gary said. "I found the almond grove. I invented drying meat. My berry yields are up eleven percent." "Nobody's saying you're not killing it, Gary." "Gathering it. Trent kills it." Kevin sighed the sigh of a man who had not been told the truth since the day they gave him the necklace. "Here's the situation. The elders met. Well. The elders and Trent. The tribe is pivoting toward big game. Mammoths. It's exciting. It's visible. When Trent drags a mammoth into camp, everyone sees the mammoth. When you bring in berries..." "Everyone eats the berries." "Right, but nobody sees them eat. It's an optics problem." "What are optics?" "Trent's word.

wp.human: "As I have taught you, to ward against this undying foe, we must remain forever vigilant. We must watch for the lies of the Lich. We must weed out his agents, lest he be reborn." From his marble raised dais, King Sigon gestured at the prisoner on the platform before him. "Citizens of Ellanaris, behold. I bring before you one who, if given the chance, would gladly turn the undead upon us all." The crowd -- a thousand men, women, and children that thronged the open square before the palace -- boomed with cries of outrage and boos of condemnation. The king unsheathed his sword from his scabbard and thrust it toward the noon sky. It glowed with a brilliant white light, illuminating the palace square below.
