wp.gemma: The rain tasted of rot and ash. It always did, these days. It clung to my ancient robes, a greasy film that refused to wash off, a constant reminder of the world’s slow, agonizing decay. Being a lich in a zombie apocalypse wasn't the glorious, terrifying dominion I’d envisioned centuries ago. It was… inconvenient. I’d been Bartholomew Blackwood, Archmage of Eldoria, once. Now, I was simply Blackwood, a perpetually damp and increasingly irritated undead entity residing in what was once the Blackwood Manor, a sprawling estate now choked with weeds and dominated by a horrifying, shuffling tapestry of the deceased. The initial reaction, predictably, hadn’t been one of awe or fear. It had been a panicked, hysterical retreat. The first few survivors – a gaggle of teenagers armed with baseball bats and a surprising amount of bravado – had fled screaming after spotting me through the rain-streaked windows. Honestly, the theatrics were a bit tiresome. I’d adjusted my phylactery, a rather uncomfortable affair involving a particularly grumpy raven, and sighed. It wasn’t a good start.
wp.claude: The trouble began, as it so often does, with the hat. I had worn the circlet of Vaelmoor for six hundred and forty years. It is a crown of black iron set with a single opal that holds the light of a dead star, and in 1347 it was enough to make the burgomaster of Thessing fall to his knees and soil himself. In the parking lot of the Fort Wayne Costco, a teenager with a compound bow looked at it from the roof and shouted, "Nice tiara, Skeletor!" Then he shot me. The arrow went through the gap between my third and fourth ribs and out the back, which did no harm except to the robe. I have patched that robe more often than I care to admit. Moths do not respect the dead. "I come in peace!" I called up, which in retrospect was poor phrasing. It has an unfortunate history. "It talks!" someone else yelled. "Of course it talks," said a third voice, older, female, and deeply unimpressed. "Hold your fire. Kevin. *Kevin.* Put the bow down."
wp.glm: There are forty-one of them in the rose garden this morning, swaying gently, like a congregation waiting for a hymn that will never come. They do not attack me. That is the one courtesy of my condition: to the dead, I read as an authority. So they simply gather at my tower and moan and stare with the blank devotion of cats who have cornered a mouse and forgotten why. I have named the nearest one Greg. "Good morning, Greg," I say. Greg's jaw works. A groan leaks out, long and tonal, like a sink draining. "Riveting," I say, and mean the opposite. In life I was Velric the Deathless, Scourge of the Vael, the Lich of Karn Hollow. Kingdoms paid tribute merely to avoid hearing my name spoken twice. Heroes came for me with holy swords and terrible haircuts, and I killed most of them, and the survivors cursed me with real feeling. You cannot imagine what it is to be cursed properly, by someone who means every word. It is a kind of being seen.

wp.human: Trying to remember what had just occurred, Steve Niemand opened his eyes. "Wh-why can't I see anything?" He said with a weak voice. A man in his early thirties, the only thing that truly stood out about Steve was his flawless, light skin. "Why can't I see anything?" He said again, this time with a raised voice. "Why can't I feel anything? Someone, please answer me!" Steve heard a deep hum as the words LIFE UPDATED appeared in bold, white letter over the blackness of his vision. "Hello, Niemand 2817. Your life has been successfully updated. You will be wiped of any artificial memories that have been stored and returned with a new objective shortly," said the soft, calming voice of an ominous female. "Niemand 28- what? My name is Steve," he replied, returning to his weak and shaken voice. Suddenly, he began to remember the moments before darkness had taken over his vision. "Wait, I was walking back home from work," said Steve.
wp.gemma: The rain smelled of iron and regret. It was a smell I’d grown accustomed to in the last… well, I’d stopped keeping track of ‘days’ a long time ago. Not that it mattered much anymore. ‘Updated’ was the operative word, wasn’t it? Life Updated. It felt less like an upgrade and more like a particularly brutal system reboot. I was standing on a street corner, the cobblestones slick beneath my worn boots. The architecture was vaguely Victorian, though subtly wrong – sharper angles, taller buildings that shouldn’t have been possible. Everything was… streamlined. Efficient. Like a meticulously constructed stage set for a play I hadn't been invited to write. My reflection in a rain-streaked window offered a grim confirmation of my state. I was still me, or at least, the fragments of me that remained. The grey eyes, the perpetually shadowed jawline, the faint tremor in my hands. But there were… adjustments. Subtleties. My left ear was slightly longer, more pointed. A barely perceptible silver shimmer lined my spine.
wp.claude: I was halfway through peeling a clementine when the world went out like a television unplugged. No pain. No falling. Just black, and then, in clean white letters hanging in the middle of the nothing: **LIFE UPDATED** Then the kitchen came back. The clementine was still in my hand, one long spiral of peel dangling from my thumb. The radio was still murmuring about traffic on the Ninety-Four. The clock on the stove said 7:42, same as before. I am seventy-one years old. I have had two cataract surgeries and a scare with my heart in 2019, so I sat down at the table and waited to find out if I was having a stroke. I smiled at the window to check whether both sides of my face worked. I said "Walter Dennis Okafor" out loud, slowly, the way the pamphlet said to. I felt fine. Better than fine, in fact. Something in my left knee, the one that clicks on stairs, felt quieter. That was when I noticed the words were still there if I closed my eyes.
wp.glm: My vision cuts to black with the words *Life Updated*. No warning. Mid-sip of coffee, a Tuesday, seven-something in the morning. White text hanging in the dark, small and sans-serif and patient, and then my kitchen snaps back like a dropped frame reloading. The coffee is still hot. The clock insists only a second is gone. I wait for the stroke symptoms. Dead arm, slurring face. Nothing comes. I feel fine. I feel fine, and that is how I know something is wrong. It takes me the whole morning to find the change, because the change is an absence, and you don't see absences. You just keep walking into them. For three years my mornings have had a ritual. Coffee, kitchen chair, the photograph on the wall: June in her rain boots, mid-puddle, caught in that gap-toothed laugh, four days before the accident. I look at her and it opens me like a door. That's the deal I made with myself. You look. You break. You get up, you go to work. Grief as cardio.

wp.human: The old Republic flag was twisted by the wind, knotted obscenely at the top of the pole. Jonus made a note to mention it at the end of the meeting. Otherwise, the outline of the North Corde Children's Center was as crisp and lucid as ever, the grass trim, the hedges pruned, the shutters an elegant black and gray, closed tight over double-thick panes of spotless glass. He remembered worrying, not so long ago, that North Corde was the right choice for Fredric's education - that the small, private school was properly equipped to meet Fredric's many unique needs. But they had impressed him then, and they continued to impress him through the bleeding of time and the rise and fall of each individual semester. Fredric grew, and grew well, never complaining or showing signs of want. The meeting, therefore, was a surprise. Jonus had been called away from work - not a thing done lightly in his particular line. But the staff at North Corde were adamant. It was *important*.
wp.gemma: The rain smelled of iron and regret tonight, a familiar scent in Oakhaven. It always seemed to weep when the currents shifted, when the Echoes grew too strong. I watched Lyra sleep, nestled deep in her silken quilt, and a familiar warmth bloomed in my chest—not just of parental affection, but of something far deeper, a recognition of the blessing she was. Lyra didn’t speak, not in the way most children do. She didn’t babble or coo or demand attention. Instead, she *felt*. She felt the tremor of the earth before the tremors were registered, the approaching storm before the clouds gathered, the loneliness of a stranger across the square. She was an Echo, a conduit to the world's quiet grief, and in Oakhaven, Echoes were revered. It hadn’t always been this way. My parents, my grandparents – they’d lived in a time of fear, of whispers and shunning. My mother had borne Lyra, and when the child began to react to everything, to absorb the sadness and anxieties of the town, they’d panicked.
wp.claude: The first time a stranger knelt in front of my daughter, she was four and had dropped her ice cream. It was strawberry, and it hit the pavement outside the Okafor creamery with a sound like a wet hand slapping a table, and Wren looked at it for one long second before her face folded in on itself. I knew that second. I had been dreading it for four years. My body went cold and quick the way it used to when I was a boy and my father's truck turned into the drive, and I was already crouching, already saying *hey, hey, it's just ice cream, we don't, Wren, we don't do that in public*, when the woman in the green coat got down on both knees on the sidewalk beside us. She didn't say anything. She held out her cupped hands under Wren's chin, the way you'd hold them under a tap. Wren was too surprised to stop.
wp.glm: My daughter was born crazed. Not mad—crazed the way temple cups are crazed, the way good glaze goes after forty years of holding hot things: a fine web of splits and plates covering all of her, from scalp to sole. The midwife turned her toward the lantern and the light fell into the crevices and lit her up like a map of somewhere no one had been. For one breath— I have never said this aloud— I felt the thing mothers must feel in the far countries, where such children are hidden away or pitied or worse. One cold breath of wrongness. Then the midwife knelt. Then my own mother knelt, and the neighbor women were fetched in out of the dark to kneel, and my daughter, six minutes old and light as a loaf, was already holier than anyone I had ever met. The priests came at dawn with their ash pots and their ledgers. They read her the way they read kiln tiles. This line means patience. This crossing means rain.

wp.human: -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- I would stare at the horizon for years after my father died, with my jaw tightly set and my fists clenched. It was the horizon that he crossed; it was the horizon that killed him. "Jay." I turned; it was Alex approaching me with his clipboard and tablet -- he wore an unusually deep scowl on his face. "We need to talk." My eyes closed. It was almost darker than the horizon. Almost. I breathed the warm, sweet air deeply. All around me there was life. The luminous flowers, like little suns, more valuable than gold itself, had always calmed me in the past. "There hasn't been a supply drop in three months, according to the Nationals. They're not landing in the right places." I retched and sneezed with enough force to make me stumble backwards. Too bad I'm allergic to the damn things. I wiped my nose and groaned. "Don't say that, don't *say* that."
wp.gemma: The shuttle shuddered, a familiar protest against atmospheric entry, and the panoramic viewscreen flickered to life, resolving into a breathtaking, impossible sight. Below us sprawled a world bathed in an eternal, golden afternoon. Verdant plains stretched to meet turquoise oceans, punctuated by towering, crystalline mountains that reflected the unrelenting sunlight. It was Eden, distilled and delivered – designated Kepler-186f-B, but quickly dubbed ‘Solara’ by the team. “Readings are stable, Captain,” Lieutenant Reyes reported, her voice crisp and professional despite the evident awe etched on her face. “Atmosphere breathable, gravity 0.98 Terran standard. Temperature consistent across the day zone. Minimal seismic activity.” Captain Eva Rostova took a deep breath, the recycled air tasting sterile and faintly metallic. Twenty years. Twenty years they’d spent scouring the cosmos, chasing the ghost of a second Earth. And here it was, a perfect, static mirror. “Prepare a scouting team,” she ordered, her voice tight with restrained excitement. “Priority: assess the day zone. Secure a landing site. And… send a preliminary drone to the twilight zone.” The day zone, of course, was the draw.
wp.claude: My daughter was four when she asked me what dark was, and I realized I had no way to explain it to someone who had never seen a shadow longer than her own feet. Pell was born at Noon. Everyone born on Hesper is born at Noon, because that is where the colony sits: on the one point of the planet where the sun hangs straight overhead and has hung there, unmoving, for perhaps four billion years. At Noon there is no morning. There is no evening. We sleep under blackout cloth stretched between the eaves, and the children think of sleep as something you do inside a tent, the way you might think of swimming as something you do inside water. "Dark is when the light goes away," I told her. "Where does it go?" I pointed out past the orchards and the warm, slow rivers, toward the horizon where the sky was a fraction paler than it was overhead. "That way. Very far." She considered this for a while. Then she said, "Can you bring some back?"
wp.glm: The wind on Halcyon only blows one direction. It lifts off the sunlit ocean at noon, crosses the white beaches and the orchards, and pours itself into the dark. Four hundred of us make our living along that border, in the settlements of the Gloaming: mirror-farmers, wind-wrights, and couriers like me who find the endless afternoon of Noon unbearable — too bright, too still, like living inside a held note. I run cargo into Midnight. Everyone else lives in Noon. You've seen the broadcasts: warm shallows, fruit that ripens while you watch, weather so kind it has never once needed forecasting. Halcyon doesn't spin; one face hangs forever toward its sun, the way the Moon hangs toward Earth, and that face is paradise. The astronomers called it tidal locking and moved on to the next line of the survey. The first colony ships made the crossing inside a single lifetime, which everyone took as a promise.

wp.human: "JESUS CHRIST, WHAT ARE YOU DOING?" I shouted as soon as the gag in my mouth was untied. "LET ME GO!" "Miss, please calm down so we can explain." The man closest to me said in a soothing voice. "YOU JUST TIED ME UP AND THREW ME INTO THE BACK OF A VAN. I'M PRETTY JUSTIFIED IN BEING PISSED OFF." "Miss Snow, you have been taken into custody by the Special Forces of the US Army. I suggest that you calm down so that we can explain your situation." Oh. Well. That was... different. "What proof do I have that you're actually Army, and not some crazy cult guys in fatigues. Why are you even wearing fatigues in the first place? You pulled me off an archery range. Not exactly a good place for camouflage." The first man's snicker was instantly killed by a stern glare from his... commanding officer, I guess. "None for right now. We'll arrive at the Pentagon in a few hours though. Until then, you don't have much choice other than to believe us."
wp.gemma: The world dissolved into a smear of grey asphalt and blurred rain. One moment I was arguing with my roommate, Liam, about the merits of pineapple on pizza – a debate I was utterly convinced I’d won – the next, I was being slammed against the back wall of a black van, the smell of leather and something metallic stinging my nostrils. My head throbbed, and the last thing I remembered was Liam yelling, "You're impossible!" Now, I was staring at four figures in dark tactical gear, their faces obscured by balaclavas. They weren’t shouting, not exactly. Their voices were clipped, professional, devoid of any warmth. One, presumably the leader, held a tablet, scrolling through what looked like holographic schematics. Another was meticulously cleaning a Glock, the metallic click-clack a jarring counterpoint to the growing panic tightening in my chest. The other two were just… watching me. Assessing. “Subject 47,” the leader said, his voice a low, measured drone. “You’ve been identified as… suitable.” Suitable for what?
wp.claude: The pancakes went gray first. I'd like to say I noticed something important before that, some omen, a crow on a wire or a shiver at midnight, but I didn't. I was sitting in a booth at the Starlite Diner with Dani and Marcus, who had insisted on taking me out at 11:58 so I could turn eighteen with syrup on my face. The waitress brought a stack with a candle stuck in the top. They sang badly. I blew it out. Then the pancakes went gray, and soft, and collapsed into themselves like wet paper. The syrup crystallized in the little pitcher. Marcus's milkshake separated into something chunky and yellow. Across the diner a man said, "What the hell," and pushed his plate away, and the woman in the next booth started to cry because her toddler's bottle had curdled in her hand. Three minutes later, two men in plain clothes walked in, said my full name, and put me in the back of a black van parked by the dumpsters. They didn't hit me or cuff me.
wp.glm: They took me at 11:47 on a Tuesday, in the loading lane behind the FoodWay, somewhere between the grease dumpster and my dying Corolla. Bag over the head, hands under my arms, four steps, a lift, and the world became carpet and diesel exhaust. Somebody apologized through the noise. "You would have run." I knew I would have. That was the worst part. I'd spent eighteen years feeling like I was about to run from something, and these strangers had known it before I did. The bag came off inside the van. Black, obviously. LED strips in the ceiling, a bench bolted to the floor, three people in gray jackets that were pretending not to be uniforms. No cuffs. "We're not cuff people," the oldest one said, which frightened me worse than cuffs would have. Their patches were gone, but I'd seen enough recruiting videos to guess at Bragg. The old one had a face like a shovel and tape around one ring finger. He talked the way my shop teacher nailed things in—two strikes, done. "I'll be Hart.

wp.human: Agent Sam Witwer had just been transfered and assigned to the newly created Federal Bureau of Technological Security, a new branch of government created by Executive Order 2001 in order to oversee the destruction and dismantling of'sentient' computer programs and associated contraband infrastructure. "Welcome to the force, Sam." Bureau Chief Clifford Addler's voice was as jovial and expressive as he hoisted a "FBTS, We Chomp Your Chips" coffee mug like a salute in Witwer's direction.
